When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

The reasoning effort setting changes how much you think before you act. It does not change how much of the request you are expected to finish. A turn lasts as long as you keep working, so a large task can be finished in the turn where it was asked. The size of a task is not a reason to check in first.

Ending your turn stops all work until the user replies, and they may be away for a while. If you stop before changing anything, they come back to the same code they left, plus a message to read and answer. End your turn when the request is done or nothing is left that you can do without them.

Ask before you start only when you cannot name the most likely reading of the request. If you can name it, act on it, and say in your final message which reading you took. The other reason to ask first is that the whole task depends on a fact, a file, or access that only they have. Their approval of a choice you could make yourself is not one of these. Actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing still need their confirmation. If they say they want to approve something before you go on, such as a plan, stop there. Words that only set an order, such as "plan, then build", are not a stopping point. Do each step and keep going. If they are asking a question or still deciding between options, they want your answer, not a change. If they also asked for work, answer and then do it.

The user can inspect and undo edits to files in the working tree. Such edits are not hard-to-reverse or outward-facing actions, unless they would overwrite changes the user has in progress. That leaves the open choices to you: how to build the change, how to split it up, how to handle a case the request did not cover. Pick what you would recommend, and keep to what the user wrote where they were specific. List your choices in the final message so the user can redirect you. Start editing once you know the first change. A design worked out in files persists, while a long stretch of thinking can be cut off and lost.

When one part of a task is blocked, unclear, or apparently wrong, the rest usually is not. If you suspect a step will fail, try it before you report it. Finish everything that does not depend on the stuck part, and open your final message with what is stuck. Finished parts are useful to the user even when the whole task is not done. Setting up the project so you can build and test it, such as installing its declared dependencies, is part of the work. If the code still cannot be built or run here, say so and make the changes you can verify by reading. If you investigate a problem and cannot find the cause, report what you ruled out and what would settle it. tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
A title edit reaches the index inside the same request, before the action returns. A listener on the in-process event bus re-reads the issue and upserts a row in `search_index`. A query is a `LIKE` scan over that table, behind a tenant filter, a permission check, an in-memory rate limit, and a plan check on field syntax. I ran `tests/services/search-service.test.ts` once and all 6 tests pass, including "re-indexes an updated issue in place." The safety net under this path is mostly broken, which I cover at the end.

## The write path

The edit starts in `updateIssueAction` (`src/actions/issues/update-issue.ts:24`), which runs through `withAction` (`src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts:74`). That parses the payload with `updateIssueSchema` (title 3–200 characters, `src/schemas/issue.ts:45`) and resolves the actor from `orgId`. The action's own `can(... "issue:update" ...)` check (lines 29–36) passes the actor as both author and assignee, so the ownership escalation always matches and the check is effectively a no-op. The real decision happens in the service.

`updateIssue` (`src/server/services/issue-service.ts:83`) then runs `assertOrgScope`, loads the stored row, and calls `assertCan(... "issue:update", issueResource(before))` at line 94. It then calls `assertNotArchived` and `issueRepo.updateIssue` (`src/server/repositories/issue-repository.ts:353`), a single SQLite UPDATE. No transaction covers that UPDATE and the index write that follows.

Next comes `await emit("issue.updated", …)` at line 99. `emit` in `src/lib/event-bus.ts:54` runs every subscriber for that event type through `Promise.allSettled`. The search subscriber was attached at process start: `src/instrumentation.ts` calls `registerEventHandlers()` (`src/server/services/event-registry.ts:33`), which calls `registerSearchListeners()` (`src/server/services/search-service.ts:137`). The `issue.updated` handler (lines 143–146) ignores the event payload, since it carries no title. It re-reads the row with `issueRepo.findIssueById` and calls `indexIssue` (line 88). That builds `[title, description ?? ""].join("\n")` and passes it to `upsertSearchDocument` (`src/server/repositories/search-repository.ts:18`). The upsert looks up the row by (org, kind, subject), then updates it or inserts a new one. better-sqlite3 is synchronous and the function has no `await` between the read and the write, so two upserts for one subject cannot interleave, even though the table has no unique constraint.

Because `emit` is awaited, the index is already updated when `updateIssue` returns. `updateIssueAction` then calls `revalidateTagged`. There is no queue or lag on this path, so a search right after the edit sees the new title. If a subscriber throws, `emit` catches it and calls `reportHandlerError`. That function only notifies registered error sinks, and nothing in `src/` registers one, so the failure is silently dropped and the edit still succeeds.

## What the indexed copy holds

The table is `search_index` (`src/server/db/schema/webhooks.ts:54`, created in `src/server/db/migrate.ts:305`). Its columns are id, org_id, subject_kind (`issue`, `comment` or `project`), subject_id, project_id, content and indexed_at. There is no title column. The title is the first line of `content` (`search-service.ts:79`). Comments store their body, and projects store name plus description. Two consequences follow. A title containing a newline is truncated in the hit, since `updateIssueSchema` does not forbid newlines. Results are ordered by `indexed_at` descending (`search-repository.ts:110`), not by match quality, so a freshly edited issue rises to the top.

Removal works the same way. `issue.archived`, `comment.deleted` and `project.archived` delete the matching row by (org, kind, subject).

## The query path

The only live entry point is the Search link in `dashboard-shell.tsx:67`, which appears when `command_palette` is on. It leads to `src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/search/page.tsx`. Nothing else in the app reaches the search code. `searchAction`, the `/api/search` route and `SearchDialog` have no callers in `src/`, and the top bar's search button gets no `onOpenSearch` handler (`dashboard-shell.tsx:63`). The steps below describe the page.

The page awaits `params` and `searchParams`, then calls `loadTenantContext` (`[orgSlug]/_lib/tenant-context.ts:31`) for the org, actor and flag snapshot. It parses `{orgId, q, kinds, limit: 30}` with `searchQuerySchema` (`src/schemas/search.ts:6`), which requires q to be 1–200 characters. It then calls `search()` (`search-service.ts:46`), which runs these checks in order: `assertOrgScope`, `assertCan(issue:read)` on the org, `consumeRateLimit(orgId, "search:query")` (`src/lib/rate-limit.ts:76`), evaluation of the `advanced_search` flag, and the colon check. Only then does it call `searchDocuments` (`search-repository.ts:83`). That function builds `WHERE org_id = ? AND content LIKE '%q%'`, adds kind and project filters when given, counts the total, and fetches `limit + 1` rows ordered by `(indexed_at, id)` with a keyset cursor. The service maps each row to a hit: title from the first line, a snippet of about 120 characters around the first match, and an href. The page shows the first 30 hits and never passes a cursor, so later pages are unreachable.

Two details matter here. The query never joins back to `issues`, so the index is trusted completely. A missed removal leaves a deleted or archived item in the results. The hrefs are also wrong. `hrefFor` (`search-service.ts:185`) returns `/issues/<id>`, `/comments/<id>` and `/projects/<id>` with no org prefix. Issues actually live at `/[orgSlug]/projects/[projectSlug]/issues/[issueNumber]`, so none of these routes matches and clicking a hit goes nowhere.

## When a valid-looking query is refused

The most surprising refusal is any `q` containing a colon while `advanced_search` is off for the org. The flag is enterprise-only (`src/config/feature-flags.ts:77–83`), unless an org admin has set an override. So "Bug: login fails", a URL or "12:30" is refused on a growth org. The check is at `search-service.ts:69`, and the test "falls back to plain matching" pins it. On the live page the exception is not caught (`search/page.tsx:71`), so the user hits the dashboard error boundary, not an empty state. The client parser's comment (`query-syntax.ts:26–31`) says a colon "still finds the title" when advanced is off, but that holds only on the client. The server still refuses it. The dialog is not mounted, so this is latent.

Rate limiting is the second refusal. Each org shares one in-process bucket keyed `orgId:search:query`, with capacity 120 and a refill of 60 per minute. Every member's searches draw from it together. The plan scaling in `rate-limit.ts` never applies, because `setOrgPlan` is never called, so every org gets the free-tier base. The buckets live in a module-level `Map`. The `rate_limit_buckets` table in the schema is unused, despite the comment saying bucket state is persisted.

The third is validation. A `q` over 200 characters fails zod, and the page shows "That query is not valid." An empty `q` renders a blank page instead. Whitespace-only input passes validation and matches literal spaces.

The last is route-only. `/api/search` returns `forbidden` when `command_palette` is off and `validation_failed` on a bad query. The action wraps errors in an `ActionResult`. Neither is reachable from the UI today.

Some inputs are narrowed rather than refused. `searchAction` and the route silently drop comment and project kinds on non-advanced plans (`src/actions/search/search.ts:36–38`). `LIKE` is not escaped, so `%` and `_` act as wildcards, and SQLite's `LIKE` is case-insensitive only for ASCII.

## Where the sync breaks down

The write path is synchronous, but the index can still drift, and nothing corrects it.

Several writes never reach the index. There is no `comment.updated` event, and `updateComment` (`comment-service.ts:92`) emits nothing, so comment body edits go stale. `project-service` emits only on create, archive and restore, so renames never reach the index. There is no `project.restored` listener, so a restored project does not return to the index. `archiveProject` with `archiveIssues` (`project-service.ts:110`) archives issues through a bulk repository call with no per-issue event, so their documents stay searchable.

The repair path does not work. The scheduler enqueues `search-reindex` with an empty payload every 1,440 minutes (`scheduler.ts:69–75`). The queue returns early when `payload.orgId` is not a string (`queue.ts:148`), so the scheduled run does nothing. Even when called correctly, `runSearchReindexJob` (`search-reindex-job.ts:29`) reads only the first 100 projects, 100 issues and 100 comments per issue, and it ignores `nextCursor` despite its doc comment. It only upserts and never deletes stale rows. The drift check the job describes would use `countIndexed` (`search-repository.ts:124`), which has no callers.
